Scoville Scale. A measurement of the pungency or spiciness of hot peppers and spicy foods, quantified in Scoville Heat Units. Developed in 1912 by pharmacist Wilbur Lincoln Scoville, it originally relied on human tasters to detect the heat threshold of pepper extracts. Modern labs use high-performance liquid chromatography to measure capsaicinoids directly, providing objective numeric values that range from zero for bell peppers to over two million for superhot varieties.

The scale is named after Wilbur Scoville, a chemist who devised the original taste-based test. Bell peppers score zero Scoville Heat Units. Jalapeños range from 2,500 to 8,000. Habaneros reach 100,000 to 350,000. The hottest peppers on record, Carolina Reaper and Trinidad Moruga Scorpion, exceed two million Scoville Heat Units. Originally, the scale was measured by diluting pepper extract in sugar water until tasters could no longer detect heat. Modern HPLC methods directly quantify capsaicin and dihydrocapsaicin, the alkaloids responsible for heat. The scale is logarithmic in practical use. A twofold increase in Scoville Heat Units feels far hotter than linear doubling might suggest. It is used not only by chefs and food manufacturers but also in hot-sauce competitions and military applications. Capsaicinoids bind to pain receptors on the tongue, creating the illusion of burning. They do not cause actual cellular damage. The Scoville test has been largely superseded by instrumental analysis, yet remains culturally iconic in eating challenges and pepper grading. Individual peppers of the same variety vary in heat due to genetics, soil nutrients, water availability, and harvest ripeness. The Scoville scale exemplifies how to quantify subjective human experience through systematic measurement methods.
